title: Design Front Middle Back Queue
description:
# Design Front Middle Back Queue

Design a queue named `FrontMiddleBackQueue` that supports insertion and deletion at the front, middle, and back.

Implement the `FrontMiddleBackQueue` class:

* `FrontMiddleBackQueue()` initializes an empty queue.
* `void pushFront(int val)` inserts `val` at the front.
* `void pushMiddle(int val)` inserts `val` at the middle position.
* `void pushBack(int val)` inserts `val` at the back.
* `int popFront()` removes and returns the front value, or returns `-1` if the queue is empty.
* `int popMiddle()` removes and returns the middle value, or returns `-1` if the queue is empty.
* `int popBack()` removes and returns the back value, or returns `-1` if the queue is empty.

When there are two valid middle positions, always use the frontmost one. Equivalently, `pushMiddle` inserts at index `size / 2`, while `popMiddle` removes index `(size - 1) / 2`.

Examples of the middle rule:

* Pushing 6 into `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` gives `[1, 2, 6, 3, 4, 5]`.
* Popping the middle from `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]` returns 3 and leaves `[1, 2, 4, 5, 6]`.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1

**Input:**
["FrontMiddleBackQueue", "pushFront", "pushBack", "pushMiddle", "pushMiddle", "popFront", "popMiddle", "popMiddle", "popBack", "popFront"]
[[], [1], [2], [3], [4], [], [], [], [], []]

**Output:**
[null, null, null, null, null, 1, 3, 4, 2, -1]

**Explanation:**
After `pushFront(1)` and `pushBack(2)`, the queue is `[1, 2]`. `pushMiddle(3)` inserts at index 1, giving `[1, 3, 2]`. `pushMiddle(4)` inserts at index 1 again, giving `[1, 4, 3, 2]`.

## Constraints

* `1 <= val <= 10^9`
* At most `1000` calls will be made to `pushFront`, `pushMiddle`, `pushBack`, `popFront`, `popMiddle`, and `popBack`.

solutions.name: Left-Heavy Two Deques
solutions.description:
## Approach
Keep two deques. `left` stores the front half and includes the frontmost middle; `right` stores the back half. Rebalance so that `left.size()` is either equal to `right.size()` or exactly one larger.

## Key Insight
With this left-heavy invariant, the frontmost middle is always `left`'s last element. Therefore `pushMiddle` inserts at the boundary and `popMiddle` removes `left.removeLast()`.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) amortized per operation
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: ArrayList Indexed Baseline
solutions.description:
## Approach
Store the whole sequence in an `ArrayList` and directly insert or remove at the required index. `pushMiddle` uses `size / 2`, and `popMiddle` uses `(size - 1) / 2`.

## Key Insight
This route is intentionally simple and makes the index rule visible. It is slower because front and middle changes shift elements, but it is a useful correctness baseline.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n) per front or middle operation, O(1) amortized for pushBack
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Sentinel Doubly Linked List Traversal
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n) for middle operations, O(1) for ends
solutions.description:
## Approach
Build a doubly linked list with head and tail sentinels. Front and back operations touch the sentinel-adjacent nodes, while middle operations traverse to `size / 2` or `(size - 1) / 2`.

## Key Insight
Although this is not the fastest route, it is the most explicit pointer model. It shows that `pushMiddle` inserts before `nodeAt(size / 2)`, while `popMiddle` removes `nodeAt((size - 1) / 2)`.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) for end operations, O(n) for middle operations
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Implicit Treap Sequence
solutions.description:
## Approach
Represent the queue as an implicit treap where each node stores its subtree size. Split and merge by index to insert at the front, middle, or back and to remove by index.

## Key Insight
The treap route treats the queue as an indexed sequence. The middle rules become ordinary order-statistic indexes: insert at `size / 2`, remove at `(size - 1) / 2`.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n) expected per operation
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Manual Circular-Buffer Halves
solutions.description:
## Approach
Use the same left-heavy two-half invariant as the deque solution, but implement each half with a hand-written circular buffer. This avoids relying on a library deque while keeping constant-time end operations.

## Key Insight
The invariant, not the container class, is the algorithm. `left` owns the frontmost middle, and rebalancing moves one value across the boundary when one side becomes too large.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) amortized per operation
- Space Complexity: O(n)

tests.description: Empty pops and even-length middle behavior.
Single-element states must work for every pop direction.
Repeated middle pops from even and odd lengths must always pick the frontmost middle.
Repeated pushMiddle calls must insert at size/2 before the current frontmost middle.
Mixed front, middle, and back operations must rebalance both sides.
The full value range must be preserved through middle and end pops.
Longer mixed sequence stresses repeated rebalancing after both middle and end operations.
